'''Douglas Arthur Quadling''' (1926–2015) was an English mathematician, school master and educationalist who was one of the four drivers behind the [[School Mathematics Project]] (SMP) in the 1960s and 70s.

==Life==
Quadling was educated at the [[City of London School]].<ref name="MCR">{{cite book |title=Marlborough College Register |date=1997 |page=45 |edition=11th}}</ref> In 1939 the school was moved out of London, at the start of [[World War II]], with most of the pupils attending [[Marlborough College]] though not accommodated there. Quadling had use of the College library at weekends, was influenced by Gordon Nobbs, one of the masters, and decided on a teaching career. In 1943 he won a scholarship to [[Emmanuel College, Cambridge]].<ref name="JCC">{{cite web |title=JCC Gazette 310: Autumn 2015 |url=http://www.jcc.org.uk/JohnCarpenterClub/media/images/news/publications/2015-Gazette-310-ONLINE.pdf |website=jcc.org.uk}}</ref>

Graduating as a [[wrangler (University of Cambridge)|wrangler]], with a two-year Part II in the [[Mathematical Tripos]], Quadling worked briefly at the end of the war at [[Fort Halstead]] for the [[Ministry of Supply]].<ref name="JCC"/> At this period, based near [[Orpington]], he met and influenced the young [[Michael Saward (priest)|Michael Saward]], who found him "a pleasant if somewhat owlish young man", while canvassing support for the [[Urban Saints|Crusaders]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Saward |first1=Michael |title=A Faint Streak of Humility |date=1999 |publisher=Paternoster Press |isbn=978-0-85364-965-6 |page=42 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=T9MmAQAAIAAJ |language=en}}</ref>

Quadling taught at [[Mill Hill School]] from 1946 to 1952. He was at Marlborough College from 1952 to 1967, becoming Head of Mathematics and a housemaster (C2). He was then a tutor at the [[Faculty of Education, University of Cambridge|Cambridge Institute of Education]], from 1968 to 1985.<ref name="MCR"/>

As a novice mathematics teacher in the late 1940s, Quadling joined the [[Mathematical Association]], serving as its President in 1980–1.<ref name="JCC"/> He spoke at a mathematics education conference in [[Ghana]] in 1968.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cundy |first1=H. M. |title=Review of Modern Comprehensive Mathematics: 2. Intermediate |journal=The Mathematical Gazette |date=1969 |volume=53 |issue=386 |page=416 |doi=10.2307/3612488 |jstor=3612488 |s2cid=125720720 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3612488 |issn=0025-5572|url-access=subscription }}</ref> He took over from [[Edwin A. Maxwell]] as editor of the ''[[Mathematical Gazette]]'' in 1971; his successor in 1980 was Victor Bryant.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Dampier |first1=Mike |title="The Mathematical Gazette": A Brief History |journal=The Mathematical Gazette |date=1996 |volume=80 |issue=487 |pages=10–11 |doi=10.2307/3620321 |jstor=3620321 |s2cid=189362829 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3620321 |issn=0025-5572|doi-access=free }}</ref> In 1983 he was awarded the [[Order of the British Empire|OBE]] for services to mathematical education. He married Ruth Starte of the Cambridge Institute of Education.<ref name="JCC"/>

==Creation of School Mathematics Project==
{{Main|School Mathematics Project}}
The School Mathematics Project, which changed the course of mathematics teaching in Britain, arose from a meeting between Quadling and three others, [[Martyn Cundy]] of [[Sherborne School]], Tom Jones of [[Winchester College]] and Professor [[Bryan Thwaites]] of [[University of Southampton]], in September 1961. Cundy, like Quadling, was involved with the Mathematical Association.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Combridge |first1=J. T. |title=The Mathematical Association Reaches Its First Century |journal=Mathematics in School |date=1972 |volume=1 |issue=2 |page=7 |jstor=30210708 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/30210708 |issn=0305-7259}}</ref>

By 1963 the compilation of new SMP mathematics syllabuses had been given to Cundy, Jones, Quadling and T. D. Morris of [[Charterhouse School]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rollett |first1=A. P. |title=A History of the Teaching of Modern Mathematics in England |journal=The Mathematical Gazette |date=1963 |volume=47 |issue=362 |page=303 |doi=10.2307/3614070 |jstor=3614070 |s2cid=187892753 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3614070 |issn=0025-5572|url-access=subscription }}</ref> From July 1964 three examination boards offered an SMP syllabus for the [[General Certificate of Education]]. When the [[A-level]] syllabus was constructed, Cundy and Quadling wrote with John Durran, Laurence Ellis, Colin Goldsmith, Tim Lewis and others.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tammadge |first1=Alan |title=SMP: The First Ten Years |journal=Mathematics in School |date=1972 |volume=1 |issue=4 |page=7 |jstor=30210768 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/30210768 |issn=0305-7259}}</ref>

==Views==
In public life, Quadling was known for lamenting the state of mathematics education, advocating the need for university courses which were more practical and scientific, in contrast to, say, the exacting Mathematical Tripos at the [[University of Cambridge]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Mathematicians |url=https://www.thetimes.com/archive/article/1961-05-29/11/15.html |access-date=8 October 2020 |agency=The Times |date=29 May 1961}}</ref> It was at school level, however, that he had greatest influence, through the SMP.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Little |first1=C |title=The School Mathematics Project: Some Secondary School Assessment Initiatives in England. In: Niss M. (eds) Cases of Assessment in Mathematics Education. New ICMI Study Series, vol 1. |date=1993 |publisher=Springer, Dordrecht |doi=10.1007/978-94-017-0980-4_8 |isbn=978-90-481-4230-9 |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-017-0980-4_8 |accessdate=8 October 2020}}</ref>

==Selected publications==
Quadling was head-hunted as a textbook writer at the Mathematical Association conference in 1955, by the authors [[C. V. Durell]] and Alan Robson (Marlborough College), and A. V. Ready of [[George Bell & Sons]]. There resulted his books on mechanics with A. R. D. Ramsay, also of Marlborough.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Quadling |first1=Douglas |title=A Century of Textbooks |journal=The Mathematical Gazette |date=1996 |volume=80 |issue=487 |page=122 |doi=10.2307/3620339 |jstor=3620339 |s2cid=126346561 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3620339 |issn=0025-5572|url-access=subscription }}</ref> His textbooks are noted for their mathematical rigour and thoroughness,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Goodstein |first1=R.L. |title=Reviewed Work: Mathematical Analysis by D. A. Quadling |journal=The Mathematical Gazette |date=December 1956 |volume=40 |issue=334 |pages=306–307 |doi=10.2307/3609646 |jstor=3609646 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3609646|accessdate=10 October 2020|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and their attention to practical application.<ref>{{cite web |title=Douglas Quadling OBE |url=https://www.marlboroughcollege.org/2015/04/douglas-quadling-obe-cr-1953-67/ |website=Marlborough College}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://blog.soton.ac.uk/mshe/remembering-douglas-quadling-obe/|title=Remembering Douglas Quadling OBE &#124; Mathematics, Science and Health Education research centre}}</ref>
